title: Buddhists debating Buddhists
hookLine: a book of debates with other early schools, set out question and answer
carry: a person is a way of speaking, not an extra thing

lines: YES. THEN IN THE SAME WAY?
cards: Is the person known as a real and ultimate fact? Yes. Then is the person known in the same way as other real and ultimate facts?
No, that can't be said. Then your first answer needs another look. That's roughly how one book of the Abhidhamma begins: not with a list, but with an argument.
Two voices, back and forth, about whether there is a person beyond the parts. It reads less like a lecture than a transcript of a very patient debate club.

teach.b: The book is the Kathavatthu, usually translated points of controversy.

It's one of the books of the Theravada Abhidhamma, and tradition says the elder Moggaliputta Tissa, whom you met at the third council on day eight hundred sixty, set it out to answer views held by other early Buddhist schools.
Each debate starts with a question to the other side. The other side answers.
Then the questioner follows the answer to its consequences, step by step, until a tension shows: if you say this, you must also say that, and you've already said you won't.

teach.h: THE OTHER SIDE CITES THE BUDDHA TOO.
teach.b: The other side gets to push back, and in places it cites the Buddha's own words. The book doesn't name the schools it debates; the later commentary does that work.
The first debate is about the person.

One group of early Buddhists, known as the personalists, held that there is a person who is neither the same as body and mind nor separate from them, and they pointed to places where the Buddha speaks of a person.
The Kathavatthu's side answers that such talk is a way of speaking, true in its place, but not one more ultimate thing beside matter and mind.

Both sides were Buddhists, reading the same teacher closely and arriving at different answers. The book goes on through many more questions: whether an awakened person can fall back, whether past and future things exist.
What's worth keeping isn't who won. It's the form. Write the other side's answer down in its own words.
Follow it honestly. Let them reply.

how: Theravada scholars study the Kathavatthu as part of the Abhidhamma, with its commentary naming the schools behind each view, and monastic debate and question-and-answer study continue in several Buddhist traditions.

practice: Bring to mind a view you disagree with, small or big, and let it speak quietly in its own words, the way someone who holds it would say it at its best.
Notice what in you wants to interrupt, let that settle, and hear the point out to its end. You don't have to agree.
